attributes.title: Level 3

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you create a new name variable, then drag out the block to set the variable inside the [on start] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why don’t the variables appear on the screen right away?

❓ What kind of information do you think might be stored in these variables?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Help the ninja make connections to how they’ve used variables before. For example, they may make the visual connection to the [set sprite to] block. Or, they may remember using a variable to act as a score or countdown timer. Discuss how variables are a piece of data that can be stored, updated, and used in a program.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding a new variable to store information about the user! 


Open Variables and click “Make a Variable”. In the pop up window, type name in the text box, then click Ok. 


Drag a [set [name] to] block into the [on start] container, below the code already there.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add an (ask for string) block in the parameter bubble of the [set [variable] to] block, then update the text to ask a question related to the variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is creating a variable by asking the user questions different than how you’ve used variables as a score or countdown before?

❓ What do you think the project will do with the user’s responses?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Previously, the ninja has only used variables to store numeric values. In this example, the ninja is asking for user input in the form of a string, and thus the variable will store a value made of text.

💡Guide the ninja in using the on screen keyboard to test out their project. They can use the direction buttons and A button to move the cursor on the screen and select the letters they’d like. They can select ABC to find capital letters and other characters to use in their response.
steps.instructions:
Ask the user a question, then store their answer in the new variable.


Open Game and drag an (ask for string) value block into the [set [variable] to] block. A string is a piece of data made up of text.


Add text in the parameter of the (ask for string)  block asking the user’s name.


Click ▶ to see the question pop up on the screen, then use the direction and A buttons to select letters to type out an answer on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add a [show long text] block, containing a (join) value block, at the end of the [on start] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What text is shown when the dialog box appears on the screen?

❓ What other strings might you join together in the [show long text] block?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Help the ninja understand what is happening when they use the (join) block. The (join) block takes two string values and combines them together. Prompt them to think about why this block is useful and how it works differently than how they’ve incorporated text in dialog boxes previously.
steps.instructions:
Use the user’s responses in a dialog box! 


Drag a [show long text] block into the bottom of the [on start] container. Edit the position parameter to adjust where the dialog box appears on screen.


Click Advanced at the bottom of the code block menu, open Text, and drag a (join) value block into the parameter in the [show long text] block.


Click ▶ to see what appears in the dialog boxes on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓In the [show long text] block, did you type the provided string into the first and third bubbles, and insert a (name) bubble into the second bubble?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the dialog box say when it appears on the screen? Does the text appear as you expected it would?

❓ How does the (name) variable know what name to use in the dialog box?

❓How else might you use the (name) variable in a message?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to identify any syntax or spelling errors, as the dialog boxes appear. Prompt the ninja to consider what words might need spacing between them, where punctuation is needed, and how to order strings and variable blocks in a sentence.
steps.instructions:
The dialog box says “HelloWorld”. Change what’s in the (join) blocks so the dialog box uses the information stored in the variable! 


In the [show long text] block, delete “Hello”, then type the string: “Meet my friend ”. Be sure to add a space after the word “friend”.


Open Variables and drag a (name) variable to replace “World.”  


Then, click + to add another bubble and type “!” in it.


Click ▶ to watch the project greet you in the dialog box!

steps.hints: ❓For the second [show long text] block, did you join the (name) variable, the string “ loves the color ”, and the (color) variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓What does the second dialog box say when it appears on the screen? Does the text appear as you expected it would?

❓ What would happen if the order of the string, “loves the color”, and the (name) variable were swapped? What would appear on the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that sequence matters! When the ninja joins different strings and variables, the order in which they place each block/string will impact how the text appears in the dialog box on the screen.
steps.instructions:
Ask for, then share the user’s favorite color! 


Create a color variable under the name variable. Click “Make a Variable” or duplicate the [set [variable] to] block and use the dropdown menu to create a new variable.


Drag an (ask for string) block into the [set [variable] to] block, then add text in the parameter asking the user’s favorite color.


Drag another [show long text] block into the bottom of the [on start] container, then drag a (join) value block into the parameter.


Drag a (name) variable into the first bubble of the (join) block. Type the string, “ loves the color “, in the second bubble. Be sure to add spaces at the beginning and end of this string.


Click + to add a third bubble, and drag a (color) variable into it. 


Click ▶ to see how the project stores and uses variables to tell fun facts about the user!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use strings and variables to create a message about the user’s favorite snack in the last [show long text] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What kind of message might you type to ask about the user’s favorite snack? Where might you place strings and where might you place the variables?

❓ What does the third dialog box say when it appears on the screen? Does the text appear as you expected it would?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡As the ninja is constructing their message, encourage them to think through what will appear in place of the (snack) and (name) variables, when the dialog box appears on the screen. As needed, have the ninja write the sentence down on a piece of paper or say it aloud to help them think through the logical sequence.

💡Prompt the ninja to notice how the (join) block switches to a vertical orientation, after a fifth bubble is added.

💡Point out to the ninja that they can right click on the [set variable to] block, then select Create ‘variable’ from the dropdown to create a variable bubble.
steps.instructions:
Ask for then share the user’s favorite snack! 


Create a variable named snack under the color variable. Click “Make a Variable” or duplicate the [set [variable] to] block and use the dropdown menu to create a new variable.


Drag an (ask for string) block into the [set [variable] to] block, then add text in the parameter asking the user’s favorite snack.


Drag another [show long text] block into the bottom of the [on start] container, then drag a (join) value block into the parameter.


Use the (name) and (snack) variables to write a message about the user’s favorite snack. Remember, extra bubbles can be added by clicking + !


Click ▶ to see how the project stores and uses variables to tell fun facts about the user!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a new variable, then add another [show long text] block that displays a message using the user’s response?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What other questions might you ask the user? How might you use their response in a sentence?

❓What effects might you add to match the responses to the fun fact questions?

❓ What directions will help people understand how your project works?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open-ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize this project by adding an additional question! 


Add a fourth question using another [set [variable] to] and (ask for string) block. Maybe the project will ask the user how old they are, what they like to do for fun, or something else entirely! 


Then, add a response using the [show long text], (join), and variables that will share the user’s answer back to them. 


After, customize the project in other ways by editing the dialog frame and adding screen, sound, or animation effects! 


Click ▶ to see the finished project! Test out the project with a friend to learn something interesting about them!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses variables and user input to share fun facts about the user!

validationItems.text: Use four questions to get user input and four variables to store the responses.
Use dialog boxes and join blocks to share the user’s answers.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Orange Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about user input, variables, and arrays. A variable stores one piece of information, while an array stores multiple pieces of information, of the same data type, in an ordered list. Variables and arrays can take in information while they are being created, while the program is running, and from user input. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: Save the Data
badges.description: Create variables and arrays to store and use data in a project.

badges.title: Results May Vary
badges.description: Create a new variable and assign it a value.

badges.title: Making a List
badges.description: Create and add items to an array.

badges.title: Dictionary
badges.description: Create and use an array of strings.

badges.title: Art Critic
badges.description: Compare two images to make something happen in a project.
